$ xref refs

by Alexander Panasenko · xrefcode.com

Find every instruction and data slot that names an address or a piece of text. It is the usual first step on a stripped binary: start from a string you can see in the program's output, find the code that uses it, then read that code with c or asm.

Usage

xref refs [OPTIONS] <TARGETS>...

Each target is either an address (0x…) or text (anything else). Several targets are searched in one pass. The binary comes from -b BIN or the XREF_BIN environment variable.

Arguments and options

Arguments

<TARGETS>...
Addresses (0x...) or texts to search references to.

Options

--back <BACK>
Also accept references this many bytes before a text (rustc format pieces start with a length byte).
default 1
--inline
Search for strings built inline from immediate stores (movabs / mov [mem], imm).

Examples

All examples were recorded on public binaries; see Provenance.

Find the code that uses a string

ripgrep prints searches_with_match in its --json statistics. refs finds the string in .rodata and every instruction that loads its address:

Command
$ xref -b rg refs searches_with_match
Output
text 0x492c1a  "searches_with_match"
0x183676  in 0x1835f0  lea rsi, [0x492c1a]
0x1837d5  in 0x183750  lea rsi, [0x492c1a]
0x183a48  in 0x1838b0  movups xmm0, [0x492c1a]
0x183e4d  in 0x183dd0  lea rsi, [0x492c1a]
0x183f9e  in 0x183f20  lea rsi, [0x492c1a]
5 hits
stderr
xref: load 2.0ms, total 6.3ms

The first line is the string itself (text ADDRESS "…"). Each following line is one reference: the instruction address, the function that contains it (in 0x…, its start address) and the instruction. Five serializer functions use the key; 0x1835f0 is the one examined on the field and c pages. movups xmm0, [0x492c1a] in 0x1838b0 copies the bytes instead of passing a pointer; it is still a reference.

Search several targets at once

Command
$ xref -b rg refs bytes_searched matched_lines
Output
text 0x492c2d  "bytes_searched"
text 0x492c48  "matched_lines"
0x183697  in 0x1835f0  lea rsi, [0x492c2d]
0x1836d1  in 0x1835f0  lea rsi, [0x492c48]
0x1837f4  in 0x183750  lea rsi, [0x492c2d]
0x183836  in 0x183750  lea rsi, [0x492c48]
0x183c23  in 0x1838b0  lea rsi, [0x492c48]
0x183e6c  in 0x183dd0  lea rsi, [0x492c2d]
0x183eaa  in 0x183dd0  lea rsi, [0x492c48]
0x183fbb  in 0x183f20  lea rsi, [0x492c2d]
0x183ff5  in 0x183f20  lea rsi, [0x492c48]
9 hits
stderr
xref: load 2.1ms, total 6.9ms

Hits from all targets are merged and sorted by address. Functions that appear for both keys (here 0x1835f0, 0x183750, 0x183dd0, 0x183f20) are the likely serializers of the structure that holds both fields.

Find references to an address

An address target lists code that takes that address (lea), loads a pointer slot holding it, or a data slot that stores it:

Command
$ xref -b xref.stripped refs 0x162bb0
Output
0xbfdd1  in 0xbfdb0  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
0xbfebb  in 0xbfe20  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
0xc0489  in 0xbff20  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
0xc0d21  in 0xbff20  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
0xf9b46  in 0xf98f0  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
0xf9c6b  in 0xf98f0  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
0xf9f0b  in 0xf98f0  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
0x124a98  in 0x124050  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
0x136c77  in 0x136240  lea rax, [0x162bb0]
9 hits
stderr
xref: load 559.7µs, total 2.1ms

Direct call/jmp instructions to a function are not listed here; use xref callers ADDRESS for call sites.

Find text built from immediate stores

Short strings are often not in .rodata at all: the compiler writes their bytes with mov instructions. --inline searches for such stores:

Command
$ xref -b xref.stripped refs --inline "while ("
Output
0xcfa1b  in 0xc7fc0..0xd0a9d  "while (" (7/7 bytes at 0xcfa1b)
1 hits
stderr
xref: load 602.6µs, total 2.1ms

(7/7 bytes at 0xcfa1b) says all seven bytes were found in stores starting at that instruction. xref istr TEXT is the same search.

A string that occurs many times

Command
$ xref -b xref.stripped refs "goto L_"
Output
text 0x10ecc  "goto L_"
text 0x12045  "goto L_"
text 0x12419  "goto L_"
text 0x125fe  "goto L_"
text 0x150e7  "goto L_"
0xb6aa4  in 0xb43a0  lea rsi, [0x125f5]  ; likely fmt template 0x125f5, piece 1
0xb868d  in 0xb43a0  lea rsi, [0x10ec6]  ; likely fmt template 0x10ec6, piece 1
0xb8d2e  in 0xb43a0  lea rsi, [0x12414]  ; likely fmt template 0x12414, piece 0
0xba3e7  in 0xb43a0  lea rsi, [0x12044]  ; likely fmt template 0x12044, piece 0
0xba599  in 0xb43a0  lea rsi, [0x125f5]  ; likely fmt template 0x125f5, piece 1
0xc7e04  in 0xc7d60  lea rcx, [0x150e7]
0xcc270  in 0xc7fc0  lea rsi, [0x12044]  ; likely fmt template 0x12044, piece 0
0xcc3a6  in 0xc7fc0  lea rsi, [0x125f5]  ; likely fmt template 0x125f5, piece 1
0xcd278  in 0xc7fc0  lea rsi, [0x12044]  ; likely fmt template 0x12044, piece 0
0xcd908  in 0xc7fc0  lea r12, [0x12044]  ; likely fmt template 0x12044, piece 0
0xcdb5e  in 0xc7fc0  lea rsi, [0x12044]  ; likely fmt template 0x12044, piece 0
Output cut here: lines 1–16 of 27 shown.
stderr
xref: load 497.2µs, total 3.1ms

Every copy of the text is listed first, then the references to any of them. A reference can point one byte before a copy ([0x12044] for the text at 0x12045): that byte is the length prefix of a format! template piece, and --back (default 1) accepts direct references up to that many bytes before the text; --back 0 keeps only direct references to the text itself. It does not turn off the format! template lookup described next.

A later piece of a format! message

Recent rustc (the template representation of core::fmt; xref.stripped is built with rustc 1.99) compiles a format! string with arguments into one byte template: each literal piece is prefixed by its length, each {} is a placeholder byte (0xC0 and up), and a 0 ends it. Code loads only the start of the template, so the text of a later piece, or a piece after a placeholder, is not referenced directly. refs looks for code that loads a template start up to 4 KiB before the text, parses the template to its end and requires at least one placeholder; a match is noted as ; likely fmt template START, piece N. Here every template begins with a placeholder, so the text starts a few bytes after the address the code loads: two when the placeholder has no optional fields (0x119c1 → 0x119c3), more when it carries flags, width or precision fields (0x13171 → 0x13177):

Command
$ xref -b xref.stripped refs "overflow("
Output
text 0x11690  "overflow("
text 0x119c3  "overflow("
text 0x12052  "overflow("
text 0x12771  "overflow("
text 0x13177  "overflow("
text 0x135fd  "overflow("
text 0x1464c  "overflow("
0xbf388  in 0xbf310  lea rsi, [0x119c1]  ; likely fmt template 0x119c1, piece 0
0xbf3c5  in 0xbf310  lea rsi, [0x12050]  ; likely fmt template 0x12050, piece 0
0xbf417  in 0xbf310  lea rsi, [0x13171]  ; likely fmt template 0x13171, piece 0
0xbf4a2  in 0xbf310  lea rsi, [0x135f7]  ; likely fmt template 0x135f7, piece 0
0xbf511  in 0xbf310  lea rsi, [0x1168a]  ; likely fmt template 0x1168a, piece 0
0xbf57d  in 0xbf310  lea rsi, [0x1276b]  ; likely fmt template 0x1276b, piece 0
0xfa3ca  in 0xfa330  lea rdi, [0x1464c]
Output cut here: lines 1–14 of 15 shown.
stderr
xref: load 442.7µs, total 3.2ms

The template search does not depend on --back: the lea lines without a note are direct references, the others were found through their template.

Reading the output

  • text ADDR "…": one occurrence of the searched text in the image.
  • INSN_ADDR in FN_START INSTRUCTION: an instruction that names the target. FN_START is the start of the containing function from .eh_frame.
  • ; likely fmt template START, piece N: the instruction loads the start of a format! byte template whose piece N (from 0) contains the text. The template was parsed completely, but a byte sequence can follow the grammar by chance, hence "likely".
  • ; likely fmt pieces array START, piece N: older rustc output, a relocated array of (pointer, length) pairs, one of which points at the text; the instruction loads an element of that array.
  • N hits: number of reference lines.
  • stderr xref: load …, total …: time to map the image and run the query.

Limits

  • Only references whose address is computed directly (lea, RIP-relative operands, absolute pointer slots) are found. Addresses built arithmetically at run time are not.
  • Text search is a byte search: the same bytes inside a longer string match too.
  • Template lookup runs only for up to 64 copies of a text and looks back at most 4 KiB; a template that starts farther away is not found.
  • refs does not decode which argument the address is passed in; for that use xref args FUNCTION on the callee.

Provenance

Recorded with a development build of xref after 0.4.0 on Linux x86-64, on rg = ripgrep 14.1.1 (official stripped release); xref.stripped = a stripped xref build (the binary of the home-page examples). Output is unchanged except that whitespace at the end of each line and empty lines at the end of the output are removed; long outputs are cut where marked.
